title: Stack Using a Linked List
statement:
Implement a stack of integers using a **singly linked list**: every pushed value becomes a new node placed at the head of the list, and every pop removes the head node. Then process a sequence of operations on an initially empty stack.

The operations are:

- `push x`: put `x` on top of the stack. Prints nothing.
- `pop`: remove the top element and print it. If the stack is empty, print `EMPTY` and change nothing.
- `top`: print the top element without removing it. If the stack is empty, print `EMPTY`.
- `size`: print the number of elements currently in the stack.
- `empty`: print `1` if the stack is empty, otherwise `0`.

Every operation except `push` prints exactly one line, in order.

**Follow-up:** Do not use a built-in stack, list or deque as the storage; define your own node type and keep all operations `O(1)`.
input_format:
The first line contains an integer `q`, the number of operations.
Each of the next `q` lines contains one operation in the form described above.
output_format: For every `pop`, `top`, `size` and `empty` operation, print one line with its result, in the order the operations appear.
constraints: Every test contains at least one operation other than `push`.

examples.input:
7
push 4
push 9
top
pop
size
pop
pop
examples.explanation: After the two pushes the stack (top first) is 9, 4. `top` prints 9, `pop` removes and prints 9, `size` prints 1, `pop` prints 4 and empties the stack, and the last `pop` finds it empty.
The stack starts empty (`1`), then holds one element (`0`), whose value is -3 (`top`), and its size is 1.

hints: Pushes and pops both happen at one end, so a linked list only needs a head pointer.
A push creates a node whose next pointer is the old head, then makes that node the head. A pop reads the head value and moves the head to its next node.
Keep a separate counter for the size so `size` does not need to walk the list, and handle the empty case before dereferencing the head.
